title: Advanced hybrid procedure for recurring atrial fibrillation
official: Hybrid AF ablation with epicardial LAA ligation and ostial electrical isolation for recurrent persistent AF following previously failed catheter ablation
summary:
Background and study aims
This study compares two treatments for persistent atrial fibrillation (AF) in patients who have previously had catheter ablation (CA) but whose AF has returned and is causing symptoms. The two treatments on offer include standard catheter ablation alone (treatment delivered from inside the heart) and hybrid ablation, combining treatment from inside and outside the heart, together with closure of a small pouch attached to the heart called the left atrial appendage, where blood clots can form during AF.

The HALO-AF study aims to determine which of these two strategies is safer and more effective at maintaining normal heart rhythm (sinus rhythm) in patients with AF that has not responded to previous treatments.

Who can participate?
Patients with recurring atrial fibrillation who previously had catheter ablation but remain symptomatic and whose cardiologists are considering another procedure to help control their heart rhythm.

What does the study involve?
The participants will undergo routine tests before their procedure, including an ECG, blood tests and an echocardiogram, as directed by the clinical care teams. Some patients may also need a CT scan. Those eligible for the study will be randomly assigned by computer to one of the two treatment groups. Neither the patients nor their doctors will be able to choose which treatment they receive. The patients will be asked to complete quality of life questionnaires at study entry and at each follow up.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Taking part in the study means that the participants remain in contact with the research team for about one year. They will need to make time for the scheduled tests and follow-up hospital visits. These tests and visits would also be required as part of clinical care if the patients did not take part in the study.

Both treatments are available within the NHS as part of clinical care for patients with AF. The convergent procedure and left atrial appendage closure are currently offered only to select patients with resistant long-standing AF.

Because of the random treatment allocation, neither the patient nor their clinician will be able to choose which procedure they will undergo.

Where is the study run from?
The study is run from the Royal Brompton Hospital, part of the Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust, in London, UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
October 2026 to October 2029.

Who is funding the study?
Royal Brompton Hospital is funding the study with a contribution from AtriCure.

Who is the main contact?
Dr Ines Kralj-Hans, i.kralj-hans@nhs.net

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Subjects must meet all the following criteria to be eligible for the study: 
1.	Age > =  18 years and able to provide informed consent at the time of screening
2.	Documented diagnosis of symptomatic persistent or longstanding persistent non-valvular atrial fibrillation 
2.1.	Persistent AF is defined as atrial fibrillation sustained for > =  7 days and < =  1 year
2.2.	Longstanding persistent AF is defined as continuous atrial fibrillation >  1 year duration
2.3.	Non-valvular atrial fibrillation is defined as cases without a mechanical heart valve requiring anticoagulation or without moderate to severe mitral stenosis
3.	Up to 2 prior catheter ablations
4.	LA diameter >  4.5cm or LAV> 130cc  
5.	Able to have LAA exclusion using either LARIAT or Atriclip based on screening / pre-procedure imaging
Exclusion criteria:
Subjects will be excluded if they meet any of the following: 
1.	Prior procedure involving opening of the pericardium or entering the pericardial space (e.g., CABG, heart transplantation, valve surgery) where adhesions are suspected. 
2.	Measured LA diameter > 6.5 cm. 
3.	Stroke or suspected neurological event within 3 months prior to the planned intervention. 
4.	NYHA Class IV heart failure symptoms. 
5.	Myocardial infarction (MI) within 3 months prior to the planned study intervention. 
6.	Prior LAA occlusion, exclusion, or removal (surgical or percutaneous)
